title: Bhutan Glacial Lake Burst Puts North Bengal on Red Alert, Thousands Moved
excerpt: Shintaphu Lake burst in Bhutan's Gasa district on October 29, sending water down the Mo Chhu to the Sankosh; 10,000 people were moved in Alipurduar and Dhubri was alerted, with no casualties reported.
body:
• Shintaphu Lake in Bhutan's Gasa district burst on Thursday evening, October 29, sending a glacial lake outburst flood down the Mo Chhu toward the Sankosh river in India.
  • North Bengal was put on red alert: about 4,000-5,000 people were moved to shelters in Alipurduar and more than 6,000 others to safer places; Dhubri in Assam was also alerted.
  • No deaths or injuries have been reported; in Bhutan the flood washed away infrastructure at the Gasa Tshachu hot springs and damaged roads and an irrigation system.
  • If family live along the Sankosh in Alipurduar, Cooch Behar, Jalpaiguri or Dhubri: stay away from riverbanks and low-lying areas and follow district administration and disaster authority alerts until the all-clear.

Outburst at Shintaphu Lake

A glacial lake outburst flood at Shintaphu Lake in Bhutan's northern Gasa district on Thursday evening triggered flash flood alerts across North Bengal and Assam, with thousands of people moved to safety along the Sankosh river. The lake, also called Shintaphu Tsho, sits below Wakila Mountain in the upper Mo Chhu basin and is listed among Bhutan's 17 potentially dangerous glacial lakes, according to NEInsider and the IANS report carried by Hi India.

In Bhutan, the surge washed away infrastructure at Gasa Tshachu, the natural hot springs near the Mo Chhu, damaged part of the road toward Laya, dumped debris on the Punakha-Gasa highway and partially damaged a solar-powered irrigation system in Punakha district. Bhutan Broadcasting Service reported no injuries or loss of life, and the hot spring area had been evacuated before the water arrived. Gasa Tshachu was previously damaged on August 26, 2021, when the swollen Mo Chhu changed course toward it.

Warning reaches the Sankosh

The Central Water Commission's Flood Forecast Monitoring Directorate issued a special advisory for Assam and West Bengal on Thursday. It said a flash flood in the upper Punatsangchhu — the river that becomes the Sankosh after entering India — was expected to reach the India-Bhutan border within six to eight hours, and flagged Dhubri in Assam and Alipurduar in West Bengal for a sudden rise in water levels.

Darjeeling MP Raju Bista urged people in the Sankosh catchment and its tributaries in the Darjeeling hills, Terai and Dooars to move to a safe distance. Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said on X that the state was monitoring the situation and the Dhubri administration was on the ground. No damage or displacement had been reported from Assam by Friday morning.

"There is no need to panic in any way. We are in alert mode, the administration is fully prompt, and all agencies are actively working"

— Amit Kumar Shaw, Superintendent of Police, Alipurduar

Evacuations in North Bengal

The largest precautionary move was in Alipurduar. Superintendent of Police Amit Kumar Shaw said about 4,000 to 5,000 people had been moved into shelters, mostly school buildings, and more than 6,000 others had been shifted to safer places. NDRF and SDRF teams were deployed at Tufanganj and Boxirhat in Cooch Behar, and alerts covered Jalpaiguri and the Darjeeling hills.

By Friday morning officials said the period of greatest flash-flood risk had passed and residents in the Indian areas were safe, though preparedness was being maintained and a red alert remained in force for the Sankosh system. Officials warned the river could carry debris, timber and dead fish as levels moved through.

Why glacial lakes are watched

A glacial lake outburst flood occurs when water held behind a natural dam of ice, rock or moraine is suddenly released. The surge travels fast through narrow Himalayan valleys and can damage roads, bridges and settlements far downstream, which is why a lake high in Gasa can force evacuations in the Bengal plains within hours. Shintaphu's place on Bhutan's dangerous-lakes list is the reason the warning moved quickly across the border.

Residents along the Sankosh and its tributaries should follow the district administration, the National Disaster Response Force updates and the Assam State Disaster Management Authority, avoid riverbanks until the all-clear, and check on family in low-lying areas of Alipurduar, Cooch Behar, Jalpaiguri and Dhubri by phone rather than travelling to the riverfront.
